photometry-color-001.question: Radiometric and photometric quantities correspond one to one. Which expresses the lux (lx), the unit of the photometric quantity illuminance, in terms of other photometric units?
photometry-color-001.explanation: Illuminance is the luminous flux incident on a surface divided by its area, so 1 lx = 1 lm/m². Its radiometric counterpart is irradiance (W/m²). cd/m² is the unit of luminance, which expresses how bright a surface looks in the viewing direction (per unit area and per unit solid angle), a different quantity from illuminance. lm/sr is the candela (cd) itself, the unit of luminous intensity, the density of luminous flux that a point source sends in a given direction. Keeping the correspondence in mind — radiant flux W ↔ luminous flux lm, radiant intensity W/sr ↔ luminous intensity cd, irradiance W/m² ↔ illuminance lx, radiance W/(m²·sr) ↔ luminance cd/m² — prevents mixing up the units.

photometry-color-002.question: For the standard photopic luminous efficiency function V(λ), which describes cone-based vision in bright surroundings, which correctly pairs the wavelength of its maximum with the maximum luminous efficacy at that wavelength (luminous flux per watt)?
photometry-color-002.explanation: The photopic luminous efficiency function V(λ) peaks at 1 at about 555 nm (yellow-green), and 1 W of monochromatic light at this wavelength corresponds to 683 lm. The candela, the base unit of photometry, is defined as the luminous intensity of monochromatic light at 540 THz (about 555 nm) with a radiant intensity of 1/683 W/sr. About 507 nm is the peak of the scotopic function V′(λ) for rod-based vision in dim surroundings, and the maximum scotopic luminous efficacy is about 1700 lm/W. So the pairing of 507 nm with 683 lm/W and the pairing of 555 nm with about 1700 lm/W both mix photopic and scotopic values. The Purkinje effect, in which blue-green light looks relatively brighter as it gets dark, comes from this shift of the peak.

photometry-color-003.question: Which value is closest to the luminous flux of a green laser pointer with a wavelength of 532 nm and an output of 5 mW? (Take V(532 nm) = 0.88 and the maximum luminous efficacy as 683 lm/W.)
photometry-color-003.explanation: The luminous flux of monochromatic light is Φv = 683 lm/W × V(λ) × Φe. Φv = 683 × 0.88 × 5×10⁻³ ≈ 3.0 lm. About 3.4 lm forgets to multiply by V(λ), treating the light as if it were at 555 nm, and about 0.0044 lm forgets the 683 lm/W and multiplies only by the luminous efficiency. At the same 5 mW, a 650 nm red laser (V ≈ 0.107) gives about 0.37 lm, roughly one eighth of the green. This is why a green laser pointer looks far brighter than a red one of the same output. For invisible infrared or ultraviolet light, V(λ) ≈ 0, so even strong radiation has almost no luminous flux.

photometry-color-004.question: A point source emits a total luminous flux of 1000 lm uniformly in all directions. Which value is closest to its luminous intensity?
photometry-color-004.explanation: Luminous intensity is the luminous flux per unit solid angle, I = dΦ/dΩ, and the solid angle of all directions is 4π sr. For a uniform point source, I = 1000 lm / 4π sr ≈ 79.6 cd, or about 80 cd. About 160 cd divides by the hemispherical solid angle 2π sr, which applies to a source radiating uniformly into one side only. About 320 cd divides by π, confusing this with the relation M = πL between the luminous exitance and luminance of a perfectly diffusing surface. Real luminaires do not radiate uniformly, so their luminous intensity is given direction by direction in a light distribution curve. With the same luminous flux, collecting the light into a narrow range with a reflector or lens raises the luminous intensity in that direction.

photometry-color-005.question: A point source is mounted on a ceiling 2 m high, and the illuminance on the floor directly below it is 100 lx. Assuming the source's luminous intensity is the same in every direction, which value is closest to the illuminance at a point on the floor 2 m horizontally from the point directly below?
photometry-color-005.explanation: Directly below, E₀ = I/h², so the luminous intensity is I = 100 × 2² = 400 cd. The distance to the point 2 m away horizontally is r = √(2² + 2²) ≈ 2.83 m, and the angle of incidence is θ = 45°. Illuminance follows both the inverse-square law for distance and the cosine law for the angle of incidence, so E = I cosθ / r² = 400 × 0.707 / 8 ≈ 35 lx (writing it as E = E₀cos³θ gives the same result). About 50 lx uses only the inverse-square law and forgets that light striking the floor obliquely spreads over a larger area. About 71 lx multiplies only by the cosine and forgets the effect of the greater distance. In lighting design, this cos³θ falloff is one cause of nonuniform floor illuminance.

photometry-color-006.question: A perfectly diffusing (Lambertian) surface with a reflectance of 0.8 is lit with an illuminance of 500 lx. Which value is closest to the luminance of this surface?
photometry-color-006.explanation: For a perfectly diffusing surface, the luminous exitance of the reflected light, M = ρE = 0.8 × 500 = 400 lm/m², and the luminance L are related by M = πL. So L = ρE/π = 400/π ≈ 127 cd/m². About 400 cd/m² forgets to divide by π, treating luminous exitance and luminance as the same thing. A Lambertian surface has the same luminance from every viewing direction and radiates with an intensity equal to the normal intensity times cosθ, so integrating over the hemisphere gives π rather than 2π. About 64 cd/m² wrongly divides by 2π. The luminance of white paper under office lighting is of this order, around 100 cd/m².

photometry-color-007.question: A uniformly glowing, perfectly diffusing surface is viewed from twice the distance (ignore atmospheric attenuation). Which correctly pairs the change in the surface's luminance with the change in the luminous flux entering the eye from the whole surface?
choices: The luminance drops to 1/4, and the luminous flux entering the eye drops to 1/4
The luminance is unchanged, and the luminous flux entering the eye drops to 1/4
The luminance drops to 1/2, and the luminous flux entering the eye drops to 1/4
photometry-color-007.explanation: Luminance is luminous flux per unit area per unit solid angle; it is set by the surface and does not depend on viewing distance. At twice the distance, the solid angle subtended by the pupil at each point on the surface becomes 1/4, so the luminous flux entering the eye becomes 1/4. But the area of the image on the retina also becomes 1/4, so the retinal illuminance (light per unit area) is unchanged and the surface looks just as bright. The option in which the luminance drops to 1/4 confuses luminance with the inverse-square law for illuminance from a whole source. There is no reason for the luminance to halve either. The conservation of luminance — that the image formed by a passive optical system such as a lens cannot be brighter in luminance than the object (and equals it in the same medium without losses) — is also related to this property.

photometry-color-008.question: What is the main reason an uncorrected silicon photodiode cannot be used as is as an illuminance meter?
choices: Silicon's spectral responsivity is largest at wavelengths beyond the visible (around 900 nm) and differs in shape from the luminous efficiency function V(λ), so the reading deviates greatly depending on the source spectrum
The current of a silicon photodiode is proportional to the square root of the optical power, so it cannot measure linearly
A silicon photodiode has no sensitivity at all to visible light and can detect only infrared
photometry-color-008.explanation: Illuminance is irradiance weighted by the luminous efficiency function V(λ), so the spectral responsivity of an illuminance meter's sensor must be matched to V(λ). Silicon responds across the whole visible range, but its responsivity peaks around 900 nm, very different from V(λ), which peaks at 555 nm. As a result, errors become large for sources whose spectra differ from the one used for calibration — for example, an incandescent lamp rich in infrared versus a white LED. Real illuminance meters approximate V(λ) by adding a photometric correction filter such as colored glass. A photodiode's photocurrent is proportional to optical power over a wide range, and it has ample sensitivity to visible light, so the other two options are wrong.

photometry-color-009.question: Which value is closest to the wavelength at which the radiation spectrum of a blackbody with a color temperature of 3000 K peaks? (Use Wien's displacement law, λmax T = 2898 µm·K.)
photometry-color-009.explanation: From Wien's displacement law, λmax = 2898 / 3000 ≈ 0.966 µm, or about 966 nm, in the near infrared. Most of the radiation from an incandescent lamp at a color temperature around 3000 K is infrared, and only part of it is visible, so its luminous efficacy is low, around 15 lm/W. About 9.7 µm is off by an order of magnitude and is close to the radiation peak of objects near room temperature (about 300 K). About 580 nm is a guess based on the light looking yellow, but the peak wavelength and the apparent color do not coincide. For the Sun (about 5800 K), the peak is about 500 nm, within the visible range. As the color temperature rises, the peak moves to shorter wavelengths and the color of the light changes from red to white to bluish white.

photometry-color-010.question: The specification of a white LED light says "color temperature 5000 K". Which correctly describes what this value means?
choices: It indicates that the junction of the LED chip reaches 5000 K
It is the temperature of the blackbody whose color is closest to the chromaticity of the light (the correlated color temperature); the higher the value, the bluer the white
It is the temperature of the blackbody whose color is closest to the chromaticity of the light; the higher the value, the redder and warmer the white
photometry-color-010.explanation: The color of sources that are not blackbody radiators, such as LEDs and fluorescent lamps, is expressed by the temperature of the closest point on the blackbody locus in a uniform chromaticity diagram (such as the CIE 1960 UCS diagram), that is, the correlated color temperature. 5000 K is a neutral, daylight-like white, bluer than the warm white of about 3000 K. The hotter a blackbody, the larger the share of short-wavelength radiation, so a higher color temperature is bluish white and a lower one is reddish and warm. The third option reverses this direction. Color temperature is an index of the color of the light and has nothing to do with the temperature of the emitting device; even in operation, an LED junction is only at several tens of degrees to about 100 °C (roughly 300 to 400 K). Even at the same correlated color temperature, different spectra render the colors of objects differently (color rendering).

photometry-color-011.question: A low-pressure sodium lamp emits nearly monochromatic light near 589 nm and has a very high luminous efficacy, but the colors of objects it illuminates can hardly be distinguished. Which correctly describes the index that expresses this property?
choices: The general color rendering index Ra is very low. Ra is found from the color shifts of test colors compared with illumination by a reference light, and the closer it is to 100, the closer objects look to how they look under the reference
The general color rendering index Ra is very high. Monochromatic light has no color fringing, so object colors are reproduced accurately
The correlated color temperature is very low. Sources with lower color temperatures always have poorer color rendering
photometry-color-011.explanation: Color rendering expresses how close the colors of objects lit by a source look to how they look under a reference light (blackbody radiation or daylight) of the same correlated color temperature. The general color rendering index Ra averages the color shifts of eight specified test colors and is 100 when there is no shift. Under monochromatic light such as a low-pressure sodium lamp, differences in the reflection spectra of objects reduce to differences in reflectance at 589 nm alone, so only lightness can be distinguished and Ra is extremely low (the formula gives a negative value, around −40). Monochromatic light does not reproduce colors accurately. Color temperature and color rendering are also separate indices: an incandescent lamp at about 2800 K has a low color temperature but an Ra of nearly 100.

photometry-color-012.question: In the CIE 1931 XYZ color system, the tristimulus values X, Y and Z are found by multiplying the spectrum of the light by the color-matching functions x̄(λ), ȳ(λ) and z̄(λ) and integrating. Which correctly describes a property of Y?
choices: Y represents the amount of yellow light and has no relation to brightness
Y is a quantity based on a real green monochromatic primary and can take negative values

The color-matching function ȳ(λ) was chosen to have the same shape as the photopic luminous efficiency function V(λ), so Y is proportional to photometric quantities such as luminance and luminous flux
photometry-color-012.explanation: The XYZ system was defined by linearly transforming the RGB color-matching functions obtained with real red, green and blue primaries (which include negative values) so that all the color-matching functions are positive. In doing so, ȳ(λ) was chosen to equal V(λ), so Y carries the brightness information and is tied directly to photometric quantities, as in luminance L = 683 ∫ S(λ)ȳ(λ) dλ. The color information is expressed separately by the chromaticity coordinates x and y, which are ratios of the tristimulus values. Y does not mean "yellow". And because X, Y and Z are based on imaginary primaries, they are never negative for real light. Negative values appear in the color-matching functions of the RGB system, which uses real primaries.

photometry-color-013.question: Two lights with completely different spectral distributions can look the same color under the same viewing conditions. Which correctly pairs this phenomenon with its reason?
choices: Metamerism: the eye judges color only from the responses of three types of cones, so if the tristimulus values match, the lights look the same color even with different spectra
An effect of color rendering: under a source with a high Ra, light of any spectrum looks the same color
Color constancy: the eye analyzes the spectrum of light in detail and cancels out differences in reflectance
photometry-color-013.explanation: Color vision is determined by the responses of three types of cones (L, M and S) with different spectral sensitivities. Because the infinite-dimensional information of a spectrum is reduced to three numbers, different spectra look the same color if their three responses (tristimulus values) are equal. This is metamerism, and it is why a display can reproduce a wide range of colors with only red, green and blue light. However, the match breaks down when the illumination or the observer changes, so fabrics that matched under shop lighting can look different outdoors. Color rendering is an index of how illumination makes object colors look; it is not a mechanism that makes different spectra the same color. Color constancy is the visual system's adaptation (in the retina and brain) that keeps object colors looking the same when the illumination changes; the eye does not analyze the spectrum in detail.

photometry-color-014.question: The tristimulus values of a certain light are X = 95.05, Y = 100.0 and Z = 108.9. Which is closest to its xy chromaticity coordinates?
photometry-color-014.explanation: Chromaticity coordinates are found by dividing by the sum of the tristimulus values. With X + Y + Z = 303.95, x = 95.05/303.95 ≈ 0.313 and y = 100.0/303.95 ≈ 0.329 (z = 1 − x − y ≈ 0.358). These are the coordinates of the white point of CIE standard daylight D65 (correlated color temperature about 6500 K), used as the white reference for displays and images. x ≈ 0.950, y ≈ 1.000 merely normalizes by Y and is not a chromaticity coordinate. y ≈ 0.358 mistakes the value of z for y. Chromaticity coordinates contain no brightness information, so fully specifying a color requires three values, Yxy: (x, y) plus Y.

photometry-color-015.question: Which statement about the CIE 1931 xy chromaticity diagram is correct?
choices: Every point inside the chromaticity diagram can be represented by monochromatic light of some wavelength
The chromaticity of a mixture of two lights lies on the straight line joining the two points, and is always exactly at the midpoint regardless of which light is stronger

The chromaticities of monochromatic light lie on a horseshoe-shaped curve (the spectral locus), and the colors that can be reproduced by mixing three lights are limited to the inside of the triangle with those three points as vertices
photometry-color-015.explanation: Tracing the chromaticity of monochromatic light as the wavelength changes gives the horseshoe-shaped spectral locus. The straight line joining its red and violet ends is the line of purples, along which lie colors such as purple and magenta that cannot be produced by monochromatic light. The chromaticity of an additive mixture of two lights lies on the straight line joining the two points, at the center of gravity weighted by the sum of each light's tristimulus values (X + Y + Z), so it is not always at the midpoint. The colors that a mixture of three sources can produce lie only within the triangle with those three points as vertices; this is a display's color gamut (sRGB, BT.2020 and so on). Most colors inside the diagram are light containing multiple wavelengths, and only colors on the curve can be produced by monochromatic light. Note also that distances on the xy chromaticity diagram are not proportional to perceived color differences.
